segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And why do you yourselves break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For God said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must be put to death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever benefit you might have had from me is a gift to God,”

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: is not to honor his father.’ So you have nullified the word of God for the sake of your tradition.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied rightly about you when he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: in vain they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he called the crowd to him and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen and understand:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—that defiles a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you know that the Pharisees took offense when they heard this saying?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Every plant that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Leave them be; they are blind guides of the blind. And if one blind person guides another, both will fall into a pit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him in response,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Explain this parable to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are even you still without understanding?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do you not see that everything that goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and that is what defiles a person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, slander.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: These are the things that defile a person; but eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus left there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then a Canaanite woman from that region came out and kept crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely tormented by a demon.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and kept asking him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send her away, because she keeps crying out behind us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she came and bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, help me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And her daughter was healed from that very hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus moved on from there and came beside the Sea of Galilee, and he went up the mountain and sat down there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the crippled, and many others. They laid them at his feet, and he healed them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may collapse on the way.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where in a remote place could we get enough loaves to satisfy so large a crowd?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How many loaves do you have?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seven, and a few small fish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After directing the crowd to recline on the ground,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven baskets full.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After sending the crowds away, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

notes.note: This was the body of rulings handed down by earlier teachers, which the Pharisees treated as binding alongside the written Law. The handwashing at issue was a ritual rinsing for purity, not hygiene, and the Law of Moses does not require it of ordinary people before meals. “Eat bread” is a Semitic idiom for having a meal.

The Greek has only “gift,” the Septuagint’s regular word for an offering to God; the parallel in Mark 7:11 gives the Hebrew term, korban. Declaring property an offering placed it under a vow, so that it could no longer be used to support one’s parents. The ruling that such a person “is not to honor his father” can be read either as forbidding the support or as releasing him from the duty.
Manuscripts divide here between “the word,” “the law,” and “the commandment” of God; the sense is hardly affected. Many manuscripts also add “or his mother” after “his father.”

The verb literally means “make common,” that is, ritually impure and unfit for contact with what is holy. The argument throughout is about purity before God, not cleanliness, which is why the saying shocked the Pharisees.

notes.traditional: is expelled; goes out into the sewer
notes.note: The Greek names the place plainly: a privy or latrine. Many English versions soften this to “is expelled” or “out of the body,” and the King James has “the draught.” The bluntness is part of the argument, since food simply passes through and never reaches the heart.

The Greek word covers abusive speech against people (slander) and against God (blasphemy). The list follows the order of the commandments concerning one’s neighbor and the word comes right after false testimony, so most modern versions take it as slander. Speech against God cannot be ruled out.

Mark 7:26 describes the woman as a Greek of Syrophoenician origin. “Canaanite” was by this time an old-fashioned, biblical term, recalling the peoples Israel displaced from the land. It sharpens the contrast with her address to Jesus as “Son of David.”

The disciples may simply want her dismissed, or they may mean “give her what she wants so that she will go.” Jesus’ reply, which explains why he is not helping her, fits the second reading better. The Greek verb itself says only “send away” or “release.”

The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself, and its significance depends on who receives it and why. Here a petitioner throws herself down before Jesus to plead for help, and modern “worship” would claim more than the scene states. Most modern versions render similarly (“knelt before him”), though scholars disagree about how much recognition of Jesus’ divine status Matthew intends in such scenes.

The Greek word is a diminutive form, which may mean small dogs or house dogs as distinct from street scavengers; the picture of dogs under the family table supports this. Some scholars think the diminutive had lost its force by this period. Either way, “dogs” was a known Jewish term of contempt for Gentiles, and the saying is harsh on its face.

Most English versions have the woman object: “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs...” The Greek connective means “for indeed” or “for even,” not “yet.” She accepts the image and argues from within it: the dogs do get fed, from what falls from the same table.

The earliest manuscripts read Magadan, a place otherwise unknown; later manuscripts replace it with the familiar Magdala, which the King James follows. The parallel in Mark 8:10 has Dalmanutha, also unidentified.

candidates.reason: “Scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, while the word names recognized experts in the Law; translators vary between “scribes,” “teachers of the law,” and “legal experts,” and it recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts.

Recurs in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, 21:28 and Hebrews 9:13 with the related adjective κοινός; “defile,” “make unclean,” and “make common” all appear in versions and the purity sense should be rendered consistently.
Frequent across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, with versions split among “fornication,” “sexual immorality,” and “unchastity,” and it is critical in the divorce sayings (Matthew 5:32; 19:9).

The word covers both slander of people and blasphemy against God; a rule is needed for which English is used when, since the choice recurs in vice lists and in the sayings about blasphemy against the Spirit.
Recurs throughout the Synoptics; “demon-possessed,” “demonized,” “oppressed by a demon,” and “tormented by a demon” imply different pictures and readers would be misled by variation.

warnings: Verse 12: σκανδαλίζω is not rendered with a register form (cause to stumble; stumble / be made to stumble; fall away; take offense / give offense; be made to fall) and has no register-exception note.
